evening.title: Flying Stripped-Down F-15 “Silver Eagles” To Their Limits
evening.text:
Driving across the vast flightline at Robins Air Force Base in Georgia, a prominent hangar bears the title “Welcome to Eagle Country.” A row of nearby smaller ‘barn’ hangars each reveals the telltale silhouette of an F-15 inside it, which on closer inspection are a mixture of either immaculate gray-painted or stripped-down bare metal Strike Eagles. The howl of one of the F-15E’s jet-fuel starters is followed by the sound of its engines spooling up. In the front seat, a pilot from the lesser-known 339th Flight Test Squadron based here is taking one of the bare metal jets up for a test flight.

The Warner Robins Air Logistics Complex here has performed program depot maintenance, known as PDM, on F-15s since 1975 and this critical support of the U.S. Air Force’s Eagle fleet continues today. The C-5M Galaxy, C-17 Globemaster, and C-130 Hercules fleets also receive deep maintenance here.

Roughly every seven years an F-15 comes to Warner Robins for PDM in the large Air Logistics Complex hangars, where it gets stripped down to the bare bones. The airframe is thoroughly checked over, the latest upgrades are added, and the jet is repaired where necessary by the hardworking depot maintenance team.

With just two squadrons of F-15C/Ds remaining, that fleet has been managed to retain airframes that don’t require PDM. Therefore, the deep maintenance at Robins is now dedicated to F-15E Strike Eagles, with new F-15EXs set to start cycling through in the next few years.

Before being painted and returned to its operational squadron, the ‘naked’ jet is handed over to a flight test team to be subjected to a rigorous series of checks including thorough airborne testing with Air Force Reserve Command’s 339th Flight Test Squadron. Stripped of all hardpoints and tanks, with even the gun missing in some cases, these aircraft are absolute hot rods. They are by default the highest-performing F-15s on the planet in this configuration.

In this latest episode of Special Access, Jamie Hunter meets Strike Eagle pilot Maj. ‘Rifle’ Wicks, who gives rare insights into the flight-testing of these stripped-down ‘Silver Eagles’ at Robins AFB before they return to their front-line units.

“It is a rocket ship for lack of a better word,” says Wicks.

Watch the video below to find out why.

evening.title: U.S. Air Force’s Containerized Surface-To-Air Missile Program Comes Into Sharper Focus
evening.text:
The U.S. Air Force has awarded a flurry of contracts to support its pursuit of a new, lower-cost anti-air missile, as well as containerized launchers to fire them. The Counter-Air Missile Program (CAMP) is targeting designs that cost no more than $500,000 apiece and can be produced at a rate of at least 1,000 per year. The war with Iran, as well as other conflicts in recent years, has driven home a critical need, in general, to expand the depth and breadth of ground-based options for tackling a wide range of aerial threats. CAMP also aligns with Air Force efforts to expand its organic ground-based air defenses, which it has historically relied on the Army to provide.

The Sierra Nevada Corporation (SNC) announced today that it, in partnership with Specter Aerospace, had received a $124 million award from the Air Force to develop an anti-air missile under CAMP. This follows news yesterday from Castelion that it had received two separate CAMP contracts covering work on an interceptor, as well as a launch pod to load them into and a containerized launcher. Anduril shared last week that it had also secured a deal to develop a launcher in support of this program.

The Air Force first shared details about CAMP, which is focused initially on a surface-to-air capability, last year. The service has said the program could also lead to a new air-to-air missile. It is an outgrowth of a ‘family’ of programs that have been focused primarily on the development of lower-cost and readily producible cruise missiles, rather than anti-air interceptors, for the U.S. military and its allies and partners. This includes the Extended Range Attack Munition (ERAM) program, under which munitions have already been provided to Ukraine, and the Family of Affordable Mass Missiles (FAMM) effort geared toward the Air Force’s own use.

“CAMP is designed to deliver a long-range offensive missile, capable of production at a fraction of the cost of legacy systems, while enabling the higher production volumes needed to restore affordable mass to the U.S. arsenal,” SNC explains in its press release today. “The program’s initial phase will produce a ground-launched prototype, laying the foundation for a formal Program of Record.”

Anduril’s press release last week separately said the initial phase of CAMP was set to last approximately 10 months.

“The highest priority of this effort is the development and demonstration of an affordable, open system, modular, and highly producible ground-launched capability. Ground-launch efforts will serve as a risk reduction effort expediting missile design maturation and evaluation for future affordable air-to-air missile capabilities,” the Air Force also said in a contract notice back in November 2025. “A ground-launch system will also serve as a new weapon class of Enterprise Test Vehicle (ETV), providing a lower cost, rapid capability to integrate and demonstrate future sub-systems and components in a relevant environment prior to integration into a Program of Record weapon.”

The term ETV here is one the U.S. military has been using in recent years to describe ‘air vehicles’ that increasingly blur the line between traditional cruise missiles, long-range one-way-attack drones, and decoys. The Air Force also refers to the land-based component of CAMP as Ground Launched Counter Air (GLCA). At the time of writing, no separate name appears to be given yet to the air-to-air spiral that may follow.

“The CAMP system All-Up Round (AUR) cost is desired to be below $500K, at a production quantity of at least 1,000 units,” per the Air Force’s contracting notice last year. “The Government desires the counter air weapon solution to trade exquisite capabilities for affordability and producibility in support of delivering quantities of 1,000-3,500 per year in full rate production.”

The notice also said designs would have to balance “performance, affordability, modularity, and producibility” by following the “Modular Weapon M-Series approach.” Beyond general modularity, this framework puts particular emphasis on open architecture systems and use of digital design tools, as well as U.S. ownership of data rights. All of this is intended to make it easier to add new and improved functionality in the future, and leverage a competitive market space beyond the original manufacturer to do that work in the most cost-effective manner.

To date, details about the kind of performance envelope the Air Force is eyeing for CAMP and what threats it wants the interceptors to be able to tackle have been scant. SNC’s press release today offers the first real hint about capability requirements in saying the missile it is working on now with Specter Aerospace will be able to reach supersonic speeds.

“The Air Force’s CAMP selection is representative of Specter’s vertically integrated approach to developing high-speed air-breathing weapons,” Arun Chundru, Chief Technology Officer at Specter Aerospace, said in a statement. “This award reflects the improved missile performance that comes from developing the airframe and air-breathing propulsion system together. We are proud to be working hand in hand with SNC to deliver the most affordable weapon system possible to the Joint Force, strengthening our supersonic readiness and deterrence at a critical point in time.”

Earlier this year, SNC and Specter announced plans to develop a ramjet-powered Low-Cost Air-to-Air Missile (LCAAM). Today’s release does not explicitly mention that design or include a previously released rendering of the LCAAM.

Castelion has not yet shared any firm details about its design for CAMP. The company is best known publicly now for its Blackbeard lower-cost hypersonic strike missile, but it is unknown whether its new anti-air interceptor design will be related in any way. Blackbeard is under development in air-launched forms for the U.S. Navy and the Air Force. The U.S. Army is also looking to acquire versions of Blackbeard for employment from ground-based launchers.

As a point of comparison, the latest versions of the AIM-9X Sidewinder missile, which can be employed in air-to-air and surface-to-air missions, have unit costs around $500,000. However, the CAMP cost point is not necessarily reflective of expected capabilities.

As TWZ previously wrote:

“In the ground-launched surface-to-air realm, a price tag under $500,000 would put CAMP at the higher end of the cost range of shorter-range interceptor designs that the Army, and the Marines to a lesser extent, have been working to field in recent years. Many of these designs, like Raytheon’s combat-proven Coyote Block 2, which the Air Force is now also operating on some level, are focused primarily on providing added layers of defense against drones. Systems that use APKWS II rockets in the surface-to-air role are increasingly part of the equation, as well. Last month, the Army announced its newest planned addition to this end of its air defense arsenal, AeroVironment’s Freedom Eagle-1. The Army’s Patriot ground-based surface-to-air missile systems lie at the other end of the cost and capability spectrum, being able to fire various interceptors that all cost multiple millions of dollars apiece.”

…

“A missile even approaching AIM-120-like capability, in either the surface-to-air or air-to-air mode, at half the price would offer particular value. If that weapon could also be made smaller than the AIM-120, it would open up additional possibilities in terms of launch environments. A modular, scalable design could be even more advantageous in that regard, creating additional flexibility while retaining commonality in components that could help with keeping costs and production times low. Owning key technical data rights would give the Air Force more opportunities to hold competitions for various aspects of the program, fostering competition that could be beneficial.”

“There are inherent challenges to doing all this with anti-air missiles, due to the general performance required, especially to be able to tackle a broader array of aerial threats. Very different capabilities can be required to successfully intercept various tiers of drones and cruise missiles, as well as traditional fixed-wing aircraft and helicopters, all operating with equally different engagement envelopes.”

It is worth noting here that the Air Force separately laid out requirements last year for a less expensive AIM-120-sized anti-air weapon it dubbed the Low-Cost High-Speed Air-to-Air Missile. The service is now pursuing other much longer-range and otherwise more capable air-to-air missiles, as well. The latter efforts are in line with very-long-range anti-air missile developments that have been steadily emerging from the U.S. Navy.

The Air Force also previously confirmed to TWZ that it was at least looking into anti-air derivatives of the lower-cost cruise missile designs being acquired under the ERAM program. The effort would leverage technology developed originally for the anti-air optimized version of the laser-guided APKWS II rocket, also known as Fixed Wing, Air Launched, Counter-Unmanned Aircraft Systems Ordnance (FALCO).

Whether or not the Air Force plans to eventually down-select to one particular design under CAMP is unclear. What we have seen to date with the ERAM and FAMM programs points to the distinct possibility that the service could pursue the acquisition of several different types of missiles under this anti-air offshoot.

Diversity of stockpiles and supply chains has been a central underlying aspect of lower-cost munitions programs across the U.S. military in recent years. As mentioned at the start of this piece, the ongoing war with Iran, as well as other conflicts in the Middle East and in Ukraine, have driven home the point that it is not enough to just have stocks of any particular weapon when hostilities break out. Depth to existing inventories and the ability to replenish them quickly are also vital, especially in larger-scale fights that become protracted. When it comes to ground-launched capabilities, in particular, more flexible launch options, including containerized and palletized systems, which can fire multiple types of munitions, are also increasingly becoming the norm.

Underlining the latter point here, “Anduril is developing a launcher that could integrate missiles from different companies and can operate across dispersed locations for extended periods with minimal personnel support,” per that company’s press release. “Anduril is incorporating manufacturing requirements into the design from the outset, including component selection, assembly, supply chain, testing, and tooling. If the Air Force selects the launcher for production, this work will reduce production costs and allow us to rapidly scale deliveries.”

In general, containerized launchers offer inherent benefits in terms of mobility and flexibility. They can be deployed via truck and rail, as well as by cargo aircraft and ships, including rapidly to forward locations. These attributes could be especially beneficial for future expeditionary or distributed operations, which the Air Force, as well as other branches of the U.S. military, see as key to future operations. Depending on how launchers loaded with CAMP interceptors are linked together with sensors and fire control nodes, it might also be possible to distribute them further away from human operators. This, in turn, could reduce the vulnerability of friendly forces while also offering greater air defense coverage over broader areas.

As noted earlier, the Air Force’s new push forward on CAMP comes as the service is now working to take on more responsibility for protecting bases abroad and at home from aerial threats, especially drones. The U.S. Army has historically been the service in charge of providing surface-to-air missile systems and other ground-based air defenses to help shield Air Force facilities. As we’ve seen with ERAM, new capabilities developed through CAMP could well make their way to other branches of the U.S. military, as well as foreign armed forces facing the same kinds of requirements, too.

With multiple companies now actively working on interceptor and launcher prototypes under CAMP, a full sense of the program’s objectives and the kinds of threats it is intended to address may noe begin to come into sharper focus.

evening.title: The "shameful" measles data that lost the US its elimination status
evening.text:
International health authorities formally announced on Tuesday that the US has lost its measles elimination status, a hard-fought public health triumph won in 2000 after decades-long vaccination efforts. The loss had been widely expected by public health experts for months, and the decision was leaked by the press last week. Still, having the designation officially stripped stings.

After the announcement Tuesday, public health experts, doctors, and political leaders decried the dramatic backslide for the US, calling it "shameful" and a "national embarrassment." News articles point to the staggering vertical rise of measles cases this year, currently over 5,400 cases, more than any other year since 1991. An explosive measles outbreak in Pennsylvania accounts for over 1,500 of those cases. There have been 10 confirmed deaths across three states, several deaths just in the last week.

But the measles data that caused the US to lose its status—the bits of it that are public at least—paint a darker picture of where the US is in its rematch with measles, the most contagious virus known on Earth. For one thing, almost none of the data from this year—the cases, the explosive Pennsylvania outbreak, the deaths—factored in to the loss. It was lost earlier. What's happening now is a runaway epidemic.

evening.title: California tells Waymo to take the next exit after freeway mishaps
evening.text:
Waymo has suspended driverless freeway rides across the US after California regulators intervened over robotaxis entering construction zones and trying to bypass highway patrol vehicles.

California's DMV banned Waymo from offering driverless trips on its freeways on Wednesday, November 11. The same day, Waymo pulled the handbrake on its freeway services countrywide.

The move affects all areas in which Waymo operates on freeways, including San Francisco, Los Angeles, Miami, Phoenix, and Austin. The Alphabet-owned company has not indicated how long the suspension will last. Waymo says freeway testing will continue with trained specialists behind the wheel.

Jonathan Groveman, spokesperson for the California DMV, told the Associated Press that the organization imposed the ban following two incidents involving Waymo's robotaxis that posed an "imminent hazard to public safety."

On November 5, three of the company's driverless cars entered an active construction zone on US 101 near Burlingame, south of San Francisco.

evening.title: This Is What Submarine HMS Vengeance Looks Like After Its Record-Setting Nuclear Deterrence Patrol
evening.text:
When a Royal Navy Vanguard nuclear ballistic missile submarine finally arrived back at its home port on Sunday, it looked every bit like it had been underway for a reported seven months. Images shared with TWZ show the boat caked in a brownish-green hue, a severe example of “marine [or bio] fouling.” Dripping rust, missing anechoic tiles and plenty of other wear and tear was visible after spending the better part of a year under water.

The 15,000-ton HMS Vengeance and its crew of about 140 returned to HM Naval Base Clyde in Scotland after a record-setting nuclear deterrence mission. The patrol was part of Operation Relentless, which “ensures at least one nuclear-powered and armed ballistic missile submarine is at sea at all times, deterring our adversaries and protecting the UK and our NATO allies,” the U.K. government said in a release. “As one submarine returns home, another is already at sea continuing this vital patrol.”

As we’ve indicated in the past, each boat has 16 missile tubes for UGM-133 Trident II submarine-launched ballistic missiles (SLBMs). However, in practice only eight are filled. When on Operation Relentless patrols, Vanguard boats are able to carry a maximum of 40 warheads, with each Trident missile able to carry multiple independently targetable re-entry vehicles (MIRVs).

HMS Vengeance began its patrol on April 12 “and spent 217 days submerged before returning on Sunday, having left the country when Keir Starmer was in Downing Street and Manchester United were third in the Premier League,” The Guardian reported, noting how much had changed since the Vengeance left port.

“Its tour surpasses the previous 205-day record set by HMS Vanguard, and has raised questions about the strains placed on sailors and the reliability of aging submarines sent on the extended missions,” the publication added.

Navy Lookout noted that the patrol “was extended at least a week beyond what was originally planned, as the boat that has now taken over experienced some kind of issue that forced her to return to Faslane [as HM Naval Base Clyde is commonly known] for assistance.”

The quartet of Vanguards, which represent the United Kingdom’s entire nuclear deterrent, has been in service for a long time. The oldest of the boats was commissioned 33 years ago, the youngest 27 years ago.

As we have previously reported, the Dreadnought class is not scheduled to enter service until the early 2030s and the estimated total program cost of around $43 billion makes it by far the most expensive single U.K. defense program. That figure notably doesn’t include the cost of replacing the warheads for the Trident missiles.

“Basically, Britain needs more boats. At least one,” urged William Alberque, an analyst for the Pacific Forum.

“The stress on the system is too much and the short-term savings of not maintaining six instead of four means longer term costs on the force and the hulls,” he told us.

The concern about longer deployments is not unique to the Royal Navy. As we have frequently noted in stories about the U.S. Navy, the longer vessels remain deployed, the longer they typically have to spend in port afterward for maintenance. This all has very worrisome cascading impacts on even routine maintenance cycles, let alone deep overhauls and upgrade efforts, as well as personnel management matters, as we have explored in detail in the past.

The issue of ships looking in rough shape after returning from long deployments is a fact of life for all navies.

Running rust and caked-on algae have been something of a lightning rod for criticism for the U.S. Navy in recent years, including from President Donald Trump. This is in part due to the negative optics of such visible wear and tear on American naval vessels, especially during calls in foreign ports.

When it comes to a submarine, especially one designed to disappear for months at a time, ‘making a hole in the ocean’ and hiding out there, there is no way to address buildup on the hull and other degradation that occurs with a submerged vessel. While anti-fouling paints can be applied to help prevent buildup of algae, a technique the Royal Navy and U.K. Ministry of Defense continue to explore, anything submerged for that long is going to pick up a lot from its environment.

As for the HMS Vengeance, the photos that naval photographer Michael Deveney (X account @MichaelGDeveney) was kind enough to share with us show just what the ‘patina’ looked like on the submarine after its extended patrol.

As you can see, many of the hull’s anechoic tiles are missing in the pictures, which is typical after the completion of a long deployment. Anechoic tiles are designed to absorb the sound waves from sonar, as well as minimize the sounds emitted from the sub to reduce the chances of it being detected via passive sonar. The images clearly show areas of corrosion having formed beneath the missing tiles. Its masts are also showing signs of wear from long stretches of saltwater exposure.

Comparing the pictures of the Vengeance with those taken of a Vanguard class sub outbound from Faslane three years ago reveals just how built-up the marine fouling is.

Tom Shugart, an adjunct senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security (CNAS) think tank and a retired U.S. Navy submarine warfare officer, said the condition of the Vengeance upon arriving in port is a sign of a job well done.

“What jumps out to me is that this appears to be the dirtiest, most sea growth-encrusted, and rustiest in-service submarine I can recall seeing—and also that it is entirely appropriate for it to look that way after being at sea for such an incredibly long time,” Shugart explained after viewing the photos we sent him. “My hat is off to the team of sailors that managed to keep her out for that long, an amazing achievement!”

evening.title: Microsoft's official Python agent framework hijacked to distribute malware
evening.text:
Microsoft’s official agent framework package hosted on PyPI has been hijacked and now installs info-stealing malware, multiple security research firms have discovered.

CEO Satya Nadella may be on stage trying to wow investors and customers at his company’s annual Ignite conference, but somewhere in the bowels of a building in Redmond his open source team is likely panicking at what appears to be unauthorized access to an administrator account on Microsoft’s Github organization.

The problem package is Microsoft’s agent-framework, versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, researchers reported late yesterday and this morning. According to OX Security, version 1.26.1 was reverted to a safe version, but the attacker later uploaded 1.26.2 through Microsoft’s official PyPI publisher account, suggesting that, at least at the time of their report, the credentials hadn’t been locked down.

Safe to say, but if you find either version in your environment assume you have some account security work to do.

Microsoft agent-framework for Python boasts nearly 200,000 downloads a month and is used to build and deploy AI agents. As of those latest releases, it’s also being used to exfiltrate environment variables, credential files, and other secrets for Azure, Git, Docker, Hugging Face, and other sensitive developer services.

To make matters worse, the package never needs to be imported to do its dirty work – all it takes is a Python interpreter with the package installed to start up – the infected package still pulls the genuine 1.26.0 version of Microsoft’s agent-framework in order to keep itself running and looking legitimate, while in the background it gathers up credentials, encrypts them as a base64-encoded chunk of JSON, and sends them off to a webhook.site address hard coded into the malware.

It appears from researcher accounts that this is made to act fast, as the malware isn’t persistent and only runs as long as the malicious version of the agent-framework remains in a site-packages directory. What it does do, however, is not just look for credentials in the environment: It actually starts calling for new ones and collecting them, too.

In particular, the malware requests fresh identity tokens from GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps, and Azure itself, which are exfiltrated to the same webhook site.

“That combination of passive theft and active token requests makes it especially dangerous in cloud build environments, because even short-lived tokens are useful when they're exfiltrated right away,” said researchers at OpenSourceMalware.

The agent-framework GitHub repo is offline as of writing. It’s been pointed out online that Microsoft’s repo for ONNX Runtime, an AI accelerator, is also offline. Other Microsoft repos remain available, and neither Microsoft nor security researchers have linked the ONNX repo’s pull to the malware campaign.

“We have made some repositories private while we investigate malicious content,” a Microsoft spokesperson told The Register. “Our priority is to protect customers and the broader ecosystem. We are working to review and will take further action as needed.”®

evening.title: MongoDB snaps up Firebolt to bring transactions and analytics under one roof
evening.text:
MongoDB has acquired analytical database specialist Firebolt in another attempt to bring transactional and analytical workloads onto one platform.

The document database vendor carved out its patch of the database market with flexible, JSON-like documents rather than rigid, predefined table structures. Developers put it to work in web, mobile, ecommerce, and content management applications.

It has since branched out to offer a data platform it says is ready for the age of AI and AI agents working across transactional environments, promising scale, speed and reliability.

Firebolt was founded in Israel in 2019. It built a cloud-native data warehouse based on the notion of automatically and transparently merging and compacting files as they are ingested. Speaking to The Register in 2020, then CTO Eldad Farkash claimed this slashes the amount of data users need to load into the system, accelerating query performance and improving concurrency.

Firebolt raised $100 million in Series C funding in 2022 at a reported valuation of $1.4 billion. MongoDB has not disclosed the acquisition price.

But what will it get, and what does that mean for MongoDB users?

In a blog post, the company said: "By integrating Firebolt into MongoDB's Intelligent Data Platform, we're bringing a high-performance analytics engine to where your operational data already lives. Firebolt's engine will run right alongside your database, and we'll keep it in sync automatically, so there's no pipeline to build or manage. You'll get one platform for operational and real-time analytical workloads, so teams can ship faster, with fewer systems to operate and secure."

The integration isn't available yet. MongoDB says customers will gain access in the coming months, while existing Firebolt customers will retain their current service and support.

MongoDB's pitch is that AI agents will need fresh operational data and fast analytical answers, without customers having to stitch separate platforms together.

MongoDB is hardly the first vendor to chase that combination. Bringing online transaction processing (OLTP) and online analytical processing (OLAP) together promises less infrastructure to manage and fewer data pipelines to maintain. Delivering both without compromises is the harder part.

Earlier this year, Databricks claimed to have cracked the problem, promising "one data, zero compromises, zero copies." It works with Reyden – a new compute engine – and Lakebase, its serverless PostgreSQL on open object storage. Rivals pointed out there were briefly two copies of the data in the system at some level.

SingleStore also tackles the problem with an in-memory row store and an on-disk column store with tiered storage, "meaning transactions hit memory first, and then they roll off to disk storage," allowing analytics and transactions on a single system.

Oracle and SAP have also spent years adding analytical capabilities to transactional platforms to reduce the delay between recording data and analyzing it.

MongoDB promises real-time analytics without a customer-managed pipeline. Whether that also means avoiding separate copies of the data is less clear. Automatic synchronization doesn't explain how the information is stored or moved underneath. The Register has asked MongoDB to clarify the architecture.

MongoDB has been here before. In 2022, it unveiled columnstore indexing designed to help developers build analytical queries into their applications. The idea was to accelerate those queries without changing the document structure or moving data to another system.

Firebolt gives MongoDB another tool for a familiar job: making analytics feel at home beside its operational database. Whether the plumbing lives up to the pitch remains to be seen. ®

evening.title: The wrong setting for AI cache can cost you a lot of cash
evening.text:
Be wary of AI costs. You may be spending more than you think and end up with nothing to show for it but an eye-popping invoice.

Register readers are finding themselves on the sharp, pointy end of AI billing, confused about which costs are covered by what, and surprised by "features" that burn through credit, seemingly without warning.

Startups without the deep pockets of established companies are the first to feel the squeeze.

Sometimes, the approach feels more like an app that urges users to deposit extra cash to keep that streak going than a helpful coding assistant. Take one reader, who told The Register about Claude burning through credits at a ferocious rate after a cache setting was reset in the background.

The cache setting controlled how long Claude "remembered" requests and was set to one hour. It's a useful feature, and it lets Claude reuse material that has already been processed. Once it expires, continuing unfinished work can mean paying to process old material again.

"After hitting my $200 Ultra plan limit," our reader told us, "I bought $250 in additional credits to finish 8 coding threads."

There didn't seem to be much work left to do, so the extra credits should have been plenty. Alas, no, after just under two hours, the entire balance was gone, and no meaningful progress was made.

They dug deeper and found that the newer request had switched back to the five-minute cache "without my action or knowledge." The figures didn't add up either, so he made a request to Anthropic to explain the cache setting change and the cost discrepancy.

"I found myself stuck with its support chatbot, Fin. It described the cache switch behavior as a 'feature' and said it couldn't provide the reconciliation or investigation." The support thread was then closed. Our reader asked again for an explanation. "Fin kept closing the support thread, sometimes just 31 seconds after I asked for human escalation."

The Register asked Anthropic for an explanation, and how users might reach a human when a chatbot comes to the end of its usefulness, but the company has yet to respond.

It's all a bit of a cautionary tale. Our reader said, "The money was gone, the work was unfinished, and I was spending time chasing answers that I needed to spend building my app.

"I wish I'd known this could happen before buying those credits."

Indeed. There are endless stories of how using AI has resulted in unexpected costs. Even celebrity mathematician Dr Hannah Fry found the token costs of sending an agent on an errand a surprise. And then there are the misunderstandings when credits gifted under one program turn out to be inapplicable for another, and support teams play a variant of ping-pong, just with customer requests.

The problem is that burning through credits or running up bills that could wipe out a start-up is all too easy. We've been here before with the cloud, and it appears the lessons need to be learned again.

Our reader complained, "We deserve to understand what we're paying for and to reach a human when the numbers don’t add up."

Caution is advised. Especially when a service appears to need only a few more dollars of credit to finish off that task. ®

Cyber insurers now want proof you can actually recover
evening.text:
Cyber insurance pricing has cooled. Marsh’s Global Insurance Market Index shows global cyber rates falling for a 13th consecutive quarter, with US rates recently stabilizing after the ransomware-driven spikes of 2020 and 2021.

Part of the reason rates are lowering is because carriers are imposing stricter requirements that determine if you will qualify at all. A major global carrier recently stopped writing law firms altogether because of claims volume, and brokers expect healthcare and managed service providers (MSPs) to be next.

The newest requirement is the one many MSPs are least ready for: proof that you can actually recover. This is what insurers really want to see, and meeting the bar is harder than it sounds.

Why insurers stopped taking backups on faith

In a recent webinar with cyber insurance provider Beltex, the familiar list of requirements came up first:

  • Multifactor authentication (MFA) on external access and privileged accounts

  • Endpoint detection and response (EDR) on every endpoint

  • A staffed 24/7 team where managed detection and response (MDR) is required, and timely patching.

Backup is now joining that list, and for good reason. For years it was assumed that having backups and a green job status was good enough. Claims have shown otherwise.

Now, attackers go after backup infrastructure to make their ransomware more effective, and an untested restore can re-infect the production network. Beltex described an MSP that restored a client directly from backup without involving the insurer. The attackers were still in the environment, and the ransom reportedly doubled.

So, carriers are asking for proof. Some want evidence of a successful restore within the last six months, and some insurance applications must be signed by a C-level executive rather than the IT director to put ownership behind it.

Proof of speed matters as much as proof of recovery

Being able to recover is only half the question, because time is where claim costs balloon. Insurers, it turns out, don’t object to paying claims. They object to paying big ones.

Beltex’s favorite example involved an 85-person firm hit through a zero-day firewall flaw. Their MDR solution contained the intrusion in about 20 minutes, forensics confirmed two servers were touched, and clean backups had the firm fully functional within 36 hours. The claim came in at around $85,000.

Compare that with downtime and business interruption: a firm billing $10,000 a day that is offline for a week loses $70,000 in income before recovery costs and claim submission. Yet large servers can take four to 24 hours to restore. That is why underwriters care how fast you can come back and how successfully.

Where you recover is the other half

Speed raises a second problem: where do you restore to? Breach counsel treats the first 72 hours as the most critical window, and incident response (IR) teams need to isolate and investigate infected systems during it.

Restoring into production too early risks reintroducing the threat and disturbing the evidence investigators need. Waiting for a safe place has the clock running. Recovery that is fast but not safe doesn’t satisfy anyone.

Meeting all of this is harder than it looks

Put the pieces together and the bar is high:

  • Backups you have actually tested

  • Recovery times you can state and meet

  • And a clean, separate place to recover to

Underwriters want to know whether you exercised reasonable care, so a row of green checkmarks won’t do. Run a test restore. Confirm you’re protecting everything that matters, including the server someone labeled “not in production.” Have the business owner, not just IT, confirm the right systems came back within agreed recovery time objectives (RTO) and recovery point objectives (RPO), and keep the logs, screenshots and sign-off in your ticketing system. It doesn’t need to resemble a government audit; Beltex noted that this alone puts you ahead of most organizations.

Where cloud disaster recovery fits

Cloud-native disaster recovery changes the equation. Cove’s DRaaS solution lets teams stage a pre-recovered VM in the N-able cloud that can be failed over to in about 15 minutes, off the production network. That answers the speed question and the location question together. Forensic investigators can validate and hunt in the sandbox while the business keeps moving, with rollback to earlier points in time. Once everyone agrees the recovery point is clean, workloads can run from the cloud over VPN, and failback uses recovery agents to bring changes home.

Where to start

Insurance is a financial failsafe, not a substitute for a bad data protection posture. Start by listing what the business couldn’t lose for 72 hours, set recovery targets, test them and document the results. Check the policy itself: a standalone cyber policy rather than a small add-on to a general one, with a limit of at least $1 million, and $2 million as the business scales. And if an incident does hit, disconnect affected machines from the network rather than powering them off, so forensic data survives.

evening.title: Exclusive: Astra to go on Rafale as IAF insists on freedom to fit weapons, own-network link for 114 jets
evening.text:
New Delhi: The Indian Air Force (IAF) will integrate the homegrown beyond-visual-range air-to-air Astra missile on its French-origin Rafale fighter jets, as the freedom to fit and use weapons of its choice without needing any foreign approval is one of its two non-negotiables for the 114 additional jets being acquired, a source in the know told ThePrint Wednesday.
The other non-negotiable is the ability to communicate freely and securely with the IAF’s networks as well as its other aircraft and assets. “Both these capabilities will feature in the contract when it is signed,” the source said.
The weapons integration capability is expected to pay off, the source underscored, as the Indian defence industry has already shown it can develop and manufacture a range of air-to-air and air-to-ground weapons.
“The IAF will be able to integrate weapons of its choice, indigenous munitions included, on the 114 additional jets without depending on anyone else, and can do the same on the original tranche if required. This has been part of the negotiations,” the source said. “This will allow indigenous weapons such as the Astra to be integrated on the Rafale.”
A second source within the defence establishment confirmed this, saying: “Weapons integration capability will come with the current procurement proposal. The Astra missile will be integrated on the Rafale, and this can be done across the fleet, both the original tranche and the additional jets.”
Access to specialised ground support equipment, such as the weapons test bench, will allow the IAF to test, calibrate and configure the aircraft’s weapon systems, the second source added.
“Weapons integration will be a unilateral capability, giving the IAF a free hand in the matter,” the first source said.
Since a weapons package makes up a sizeable share of a fighter jet’s overall price, arming the Rafale with homegrown weapons could, in time, also cut the bill for the IAF. It would also give the force the flexibility to shape the jet’s offensive capabilities around its changing requirements.
“The second non-negotiable is that the software-defined radio (SDR) aboard the 114 jets must be able to exchange information faster with every IAF platform, both in service and yet to come, no matter where it was built. This has also been ensured under the acquisition underway,” said the first source. Such rapid communication makes possible what the military refers to as net-centric operations. The IAF’s current fleet, a mix of mostly Russian- and Western-origin jets and limited indigenous platforms, is already largely capable of such operations, and the additional Rafales will blend seamlessly into that mix.
An SDR is a flexible, programmable communication system through which aircraft can exchange data securely over networks. It is the basis of net-centric air warfare, in which the systems that spot targets, the aircraft that fire on them and the commanders directing them are all connected at every moment. As a result, several aircraft can share what they see and work as a team to locate, track and strike targets, an approach known as collaborative engagement. This capability is key to realising what the IAF leadership describes as “any sensor, best shooter”.
“Every pilot, radar, remotely piloted aircraft and commander must be able to see what everyone else sees, in real time, as if they were all in the same cockpit. This is also crucial given the arrival of stealth combat aircraft in our neighbourhood,” the first source explained.
This source however, made clear that the aircraft’s complete “source code”, the software backbone controlling its sensors, weapons and mission systems, had not been part of the ask. “Even where an aircraft is manufactured locally, access to its so-called ‘source code’ is not the norm,” they added. Such access, the source said, would not be needed to integrate weapons unilaterally or to run net-centric operations through the SDR.
An estimated Rs 3.6 lakh crore worth of proposals from the three services, the purchase of more Rafale jets among them, cleared the first stage of government defence buying in February this year, when the Defence Acquisition Council granted them “acceptance of necessity”. The council is the Ministry of Defence’s highest decision-making forum.
For the 114 Rafale aircraft alone, the cost has been estimated at around Rs 2.7 lakh crore, and the acquisition is yet to receive final approval from the Prime Minister-led Cabinet Committee on Security. Production in India is being built into the agreement, with locally manufactured content in the aircraft eventually rising to between 55 and 60 percent.
France will supply only the first lot, in fly-away condition, while the bulk will roll out of Indian facilities. Assuming the agreement is signed by early 2027, deliveries of the first fly-away jets are expected to start from 2030 onwards.
The IAF got its first 36 Rafale jets under a deal signed in 2016, while the Indian Navy placed an order for 26 of the aircraft’s marine version in 2025. The Rafale is a twin-engine, multirole, 4.5-generation fighter designed and built by France’s Dassault Aviation.
(Edited by Gitanjali Das)

evening.title: PowerShell 7 heading into Windows as 5.1 hits the end of the road
evening.text:
Microsoft has confirmed that, at long last, PowerShell 7 will come bundled with Windows, while the venerable PowerShell 5.1 begins its long retirement.

It has been a long time coming, although PowerShell 5.1 isn't going away immediately. It will, however, "be removed from a future version of Windows," and Windows Server 2025 and Windows 11 26H2 are the last versions to include PowerShell 5.1 enabled by default.

After that, PowerShell 5.1 will be available as a Feature On Demand (FOD) before eventually shuffling off into the sunset, while PowerShell 7 takes over automation duties.

PowerShell 5.1 is now more than ten years old and runs on the .NET Framework. PowerShell 7 is its cross-platform, open source successor, but compatibility isn't seamless.

PowerShell was the brainchild of Jeffrey Snover, who sought to bring script automation to Windows at a time when graphical user interfaces were king. He recalled executives telling him "admins don't want command line interfaces," and "exactly what part of effing Windows is confusing you?" but eventually won the argument, and we reckon countless Windows administrators owe him a debt of gratitude.

PowerShell 5.1 hasn't had many new features for years. "PowerShell 7 is the modern PowerShell: the one we develop in the open, across platforms, and where new features go," wrote Jason Helmick, a senior product manager on Microsoft's PowerShell team. But compatibility niggles remain.

The two can run side by side, so existing scripts won't have to move immediately. Finding and testing everything scattered across an enterprise estate, however, could keep administrators occupied for some time.

Microsoft also has unfinished work on the bundled version's MSIX packaging, including support for running as SYSTEM, DISM cmdlets, and machine-wide settings. Those gaps matter for scheduled tasks, services, and management scripts.

Despite the deprecation, PowerShell 5.1 will continue to receive updates based on the lifecycle of the Windows version on which it runs. It will eventually be removed based on usage data and "communicated in advance," according to Microsoft.

Administrators have time to prepare, but checking which scripts run unchanged, which need work, and which still depend on 5.1 won't happen by itself.

"Including PowerShell 7 in Windows is a milestone we've been working toward since PowerShell went cross-platform," Helmick wrote, although the bundled release is still ahead.

Microsoft says PowerShell 7 will arrive with the next Windows release, but hasn't named it. 27H2, anyone? ®

evening.title: Lockheed Martin Comic Revisits IAF’s 2021 Kabul Airlift
evening.text:
Lockheed Martin has published the third instalment of its Herculean Tales of the C-130J comic series, which looks back on the Indian Air Force’s rescue missions in Kabul, Afghanistan in August 2021. Titled The Kabul Lift, this latest addition to the series demonstrates how the C-130J-30 Super Hercules has helped India complete evacuations.
The comic is part of the promotional storytelling series, showing the tension at Hamid Karzai International Airport as thousands of people tried to flee the country due to the worsening security situation. The story follows the preparation of the Indian Air Force mission, the arrival of the C-130J and the evacuation of passengers.
Throughout the comic, the aircraft can be seen flying at night as the crew and ground staff prepare for the evacuation. Passengers have been put aboard and the C-130J has departed Kabul. This demonstrates the aircraft’s ability to operate in extreme environments and provide an emergency military airlift capability.
The events in the comic relate to Operation Devi Shakti, which was India’s evacuation operation in response to the political fall of Afghanistan in August 2021. A combination of Indian Air Force and civilian aircraft were deployed to bring Indian Nationals, Afghan Nationals and other Nationals back.
Between 15th and 28th August, 5 IAF aircraft were deployed (4 C-17 Globemaster III’s and 1 C-130J) to evacuate 132 government officials, 316 Indian Nationals and 126 other Nationals. Flights were made from Kabul and other locations with evacuations taking place from Kandahar and Mazar-e-Sharif.
The C-130J was also used to transport evacuees from Kabul to Dushanbe in Tajikistan. The operation was extremely challenging, with the security situation changing quickly, the airport becoming very busy, and co-ordination with many different countries to obtain clearances and evacuation details.
Operation Devi Shakti successfully evacuated 565 people during August 2021 and a further flight was completed in December. This highlighted the importance of India’s strategic airlift capabilities to perform non-combatant evacuations from far away locations.
The C-130J-30 is used by the Indian Air Force to provide tactical airlift, special operations and humanitarian missions. Due to its ability to operate from short and rough runways, it is extremely useful for missions where traditional transport aircraft may not be able to operate.

evening.title: AI-powered cyber threats are changing the rules of enterprise recovery
evening.text:
Cybersecurity has long been a contest between attackers finding new ways in and defenders trying to keep them out. Artificial intelligence is making that contest more complicated, giving cybercriminals new ways to develop and adapt their attacks while putting additional pressure on conventional cyber defences.

For enterprise IT leaders, the challenge extends beyond preventing a breach. What happens when an attacker gets through? Can compromised data be identified, clean copies recovered, and essential systems brought back online without prolonged disruption?

These questions are becoming increasingly important as organizations confront both traditional threats and emerging AI-powered cyberattacks. A successful defense strategy must, therefore, account for what happens after an incident, not just the measures designed to prevent one.

Making recovery part of the defence

This is where cyber-resilient enterprise storage has an important role to play. Rather than relying solely on traditional backup processes, organizations need ways to protect critical data, detect potential compromise, establish which copies can safely be recovered, and restore those copies as quickly as possible.

Infinidat addresses this challenge through its InfiniBox and InfiniBox SSA enterprise storage platforms, which incorporate the company’s InfiniSafe cyber resilience and recovery software suite.

InfiniSafe combines immutable snapshots, which cannot be altered or deleted during their protected retention period, with logical air-gapping to isolate the management plane from the data plane. Fenced forensic environments provide a separate space for validating data before recovery.

The technology also supports automated cyber protection, allowing security monitoring data center wide cyber security software applications or a Security Operations Center (SOC) to automatically talk to InfiniBoxes and trigger immutable snapshots when suspicious activity is detected. This helps reduce the window in which critical data might be exposed.

For organizations concerned about recovering compromised information, optional InfiniSafe Cyber Detection uses AI-based analysis to help identify cyber affected data and locate the last known good copy of the data for recovery.

Speed is another consideration. Infinidat guarantees recovery of immutable snapshots in one minute or less for InfiniBox and InfiniBox SSA, subject to the guarantee’s terms and conditions.

Ultimately, cyber resilience isn’t about assuming every cyberattack can be stopped. It’s about ensuring that when defences are breached, organizations have the tools and processes to recover trusted data and limit the operational consequences.

For enterprise IT teams, that makes recovery readiness an essential part of the cybersecurity conversation.

evening.title: DRDO Explores Lithium-Ion Batteries for Future Torpedoes
evening.text:
The Defence Research and Development Organisation’s Naval Science and Technological Laboratory has created a battery exhibit at Visakhapatnam, showcasing six electrochemical technologies for batteries used in Indian naval applications. The exhibit, called URJAAYAN which translates to energy journey, showcases some of the cutting edge technologies being used in India’s underwater weaponry and the direction research will take in the future.
The exhibit was opened on 30 th July 2026 by Dr R.V. Hara Prasad, Distinguished Scientist and Director General (Naval Systems and Materials). The event was attended by Dr Abraham Varughese, NSTL Director, and Technology Director Dr T.V.S.L. Satyavani. The exhibit showcases battery technologies and models of systems developed by the laboratory for use in naval batteries. The goal of the exhibit is to increase understanding of existing technologies and show what the future holds (DRDO, 2026).
The exhibit features a number of battery chemistries including Zn-AgO, Al-AgO, Mg-AgCl, Mg-CuCl, Thermal Reserve Lithium and Li-ion. Each of these batteries have different uses, from single use batteries for torpedoes to rechargeable batteries and long-life batteries.
Silver-zinc batteries continue to play an important role in high power torpedo propulsion. A 250kW secondary silver oxide zinc battery has been developed by DRDO containing zinc as the anode, silver oxide as the cathode and potassium hydroxide as the electrolyte. This battery can supply high power at 400 volts, 625 amps for 5 minutes. This increased the propulsion power available from 100kW to 250kW in a roughly similar volume (DRDO, 2007).
However, silver-zinc batteries do have some issues. They do not have very long cycle life and require maintenance. Due to their high power they are useful for high power torpedo applications. However, due to the cost of silver and the limited recharging capabilities of the batteries there is an incentive to find new alternatives.
Magnesium silver chloride batteries are useful for lighter torpedoes. This is a seawater activated reserve battery. During storage the battery will not be active but when seawater comes into contact with the battery it will start to produce electricity. NSTL has developed a 50kW Mg-AgCl battery using their MTA-75 magnesium thallium alloy. It was reported that this alloy had increased the voltage of the cells by around 15% compared with their previous AP-65 alloy. This allowed for higher currents to be supplied (DRDO).
The exhibit also contains Magnesium cuprous chloride. This is another seawater activated battery. This is significant as it provides an alternative to silver cathodes.
Aluminium silver oxide batteries are another high rate battery using seawater. These would be useful for lightweight torpedo propulsion. However, details of the battery developed by NSTL have not been published.
The last two battery types are both lithium based. Lithium thermal reserve batteries are primary batteries that use a heat source to melt the salt electrolyte. As they are able to be stored without activating they are useful for applications such as fuze, safe and arm and guidance systems requiring long life.
Lithium ion batteries are rechargeable and could be used to support exercise torpedoes, autonomous underwater vehicles and other reusable applications.
A study conducted by NSTL researchers looked into the viability of lithium ion batteries for use in light and heavy torpedoes (2023). This study looked into the configuration of the battery and found that commercially available lithium ion cells could partially meet the requirements. For one of the lightweight torpedo configurations it was found that the battery could supply 50.4kW compared to the requirement of 75kW.
It was also found that lithium ion batteries could be cheaper than silver oxide zinc batteries after more than 100 cycles. On average there was an order of magnitude difference in price. This means rechargeable batteries could be useful for systems that will require many tests. However, they may not yet be able to replace the high power single use batteries.

evening.title: Space robot legend Voyager 1 is now more than 1 light-day away
evening.text:
NASA's Voyager 1 probe is now more than one light-day from Earth – so distant that a radio signal takes 24 hours to reach it. The veteran spacecraft has spent almost 50 years getting there.

Voyager 1 was launched on September 5, 1977, from Cape Canaveral in Florida. Planning for the mission began in the 1960s, while NASA was working feverishly to put a man on the Moon ahead of the Soviet Union.

A rare alignment of the outer planets made a tour of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune possible. Voyager 2 eventually visited all four; Voyager 1's route prioritized Saturn's moon Titan, ruling out a subsequent encounter with Pluto.

Voyager 1 completed a flyby of Jupiter in 1979, and passed Saturn and Titan in 1980. Its final imaging sequence in 1990 produced the solar system "Family Portrait," including the famous Pale Blue Dot image of Earth. The cameras were then switched off for good.

Thirty-six years after those final pictures, Voyager 1 remains in contact with Earth, with two science instruments still operating: the magnetometer and plasma wave subsystem. Others have been shut down over the decades to conserve the dwindling power supplied by its radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs).

Dr Garry Hunt, a member of Voyager's original imaging team, told The Register: "Voyager's real success is the way it used reliable equipment. Well-tested Mariner equipment, and special new things that had come about for it.

"We had fault protection on board as well. If anything goes wrong, it automatically switches to a backup. So there was always a backup. There was always a safe mode. We had to have radiation protection on board … when we designed this, we didn't really know the magnetic environment around Jupiter, and to be told it was so strong, 1,000 times stronger than we anticipated, really threw everything up in the air, and so that had to be dealt with."

Hunt paid tribute to the succession of project managers and engineers who have kept the probe running over the years. "I think this was a really wonderful example of project management, of clever management of engineering, and interesting science coming out of it, which has made history books and gone to be a catalyst for other things in the future," he said.

Voyager 1 may now take two days to answer a call from Earth. After almost 50 years, the remarkable thing is that it still answers at all. ®

Bhairav Robotics has carried out desert testing for the Vrishabh Combat UGV. It has tested the system across tough terrain such as sand dunes, loose dirt, gravel and uneven surfaces. The unmanned platform can also operate alongside tanks.
The testing aims to evaluate how well the UGV can perform in challenging desert conditions. The Vrishabh is doing well, however unmanned combat testing will be conducted next.
The fact it is being tested alongside tanks is very relevant as the idea of manned / unmanned collaboration can be implemented. In future battlefields, the UGV can potentially be used with armour to carry out surveillance, logistics and support operations. This can be done in areas where it would not be ideal to put people in harms way. However, the company has not mentioned what level of coordination and autonomy was carried out.
The Vrishabh is a four wheeled modular combat UGV produced by Bhairav Robotics. It can be used for defence and homeland security and has several roles including front line support, border patrol, surveillance, bomb disposal, logistics and casualty evacuation.
As per the companies specifications, the Vrishabh can travel at speeds of up to 50km/h and has a range of around 100km. The UGV can run for up to 6 hours. It can carry payloads of 150kg.
It is capable of operating in manual, semi autonomous and autonomous modes. The UGV is modular so can have sensor, logistics and weaponry fitted. Janes previously reported that the Vrishabh is being developed to have the option to fit machine guns and grenade launchers. This includes their Rakshak remote weapon station.
Testing in the desert is an important step to ensure the UGV can be relied upon to operate in conditions similar to those on Indias western borders. Looser sand and sand dunes will present challenges for a small wheeled platform. Dust and high temperatures can also be a problem for electronics, batteries and mechanical parts.
Next stages of testing will see unmanned combat testing carried out. This will be a much bigger step to ensure the UGV can be used on the battlefield. Testing should show that it can be reliably operated remotely, navigate and communicate. It should also be able to overcome obstacles and safely fit payloads.

evening.title: Business as usual, but Huang ain't coming back, says Nvidia
evening.text:
Nvidia's board says it has no plans to bring Jensen Huang back as the GPU giant reports quarterly revenue more than double that of a year ago.

The AI infrastructure leviathan had some reassuring to do after its leather-jacketed rockstar leader left under a cloud last week. Huang had been central to its rise as the dominant supplier of AI compute.

Newly appointed board chair Harvey Jones ruled out an imminent comeback, saying: "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."

Jones said the board was addressing the fallout and strengthening oversight, pointing to the creation of a committee to scrutinize the firm's security policies and export compliance.

Nvidia has also retained the services of talent spotters Heidrick & Struggles to help find a new leader, according to Jones.

Interim CEO and chief financial officer Colette Kress struck an upbeat tone on the company's Q3 earnings call. The results gave her plenty to work with: revenue rose 103 percent to $115.8 billion, while operating income climbed 115 percent to $77.5 billion.

"We're addressing strong demand for compute across a diverse and expansive set of end customers, including hyperscalers, frontier labs, AI natives, enterprises, and governments," Kress said. She raised Nvidia's outlook for fiscal 2028, saying that the firm now expects revenue to grow approximately 75 percent year-on-year.

Analysts immediately questioned this, asking what gave Kress the confidence to raise the outlook, given all the uncertainty surrounding the future direction of the company.

Kress cited growing demand and additional supply as reasons for lifting the fiscal 2028 growth forecast from 70 to 75 percent.

When asked about the financing deals that Nvidia provides for some of its customers, Kress appeared to hint that some things might change.

"Our neoclouds have been so instrumental in terms of both supporting enterprises and supporting many of the different countries around the world, particularly on the sovereign perspective. And we continue to be working with them," she stated.

But she added: "I think we would look at this and take a very strong look in terms of the types of companies that we would want to help in terms of the financing, as a lot of things have changed over this last quarter... but we do have some very, very strong existing customers that we will be continuing to work with."

Kress also said that Nvidia's rack-scale Rubin platform had generated nearly $20 billion in revenue in its first quarter of production shipments. She said the firm expects the major frontier AI labs to account for approximately 15 percent of its Data Center revenue this year.

Kress said that Nvidia is no longer shipping licensed products based on its Hopper silicon to China, as scrutiny grows over Beijing's access to advanced AI technology, and so its future guidance does not count on any Hopper revenue from there.

Nvidia sold $2.4 billion worth of Hopper kit to China during Q3 after being given the go-ahead from the Trump administration to sell products like its H200 accelerators in China.

Analysts say they expect doubts to remain over Nvidia's future despite the strong Q3 results as the quarter was already in the bag by the time the Huang scandal broke.

"Nvidia's next battle is not against competitors alone. It must navigate export controls, sovereign AI initiatives, supply chain expansion, and rising capital intensity – all while protecting industry-leading margins," commented Forrester principal analyst Naveen Chhabra.

"The market sees the biggest risk not in the financials, but the leadership and employee motivation amidst turmoil, which began only after the Q3 ended. The bigger risk is not near-term demand but operations, maintaining employee confidence, retaining talent, and preserving Nvidia's innovation culture."

February's results should offer a clearer view of Nvidia after Huang. For now, the mighty AI platform biz expects another record quarter, forecasting revenue of $130 billion, give or take 3 percent. ®

evening.title: Russian Analysts Examine Rafale-M’s Vikrant Landing
evening.text:
The Rafale-M landing successfully on the INS Vikrant on 29 October marks a significant step forward in the integration of the French multirole fighter onto the Indian carriers. However, Russian defence publications have highlighted some interesting points regarding the actual takeoff profile of the aircraft, the differences between ski jump and catapult takeoffs, and the industrial benefits France gains.
The Centre for Analysis of World Arms Trade (ЦАМТО) published an in-depth report on 2 November. This report highlighted the successful carrier trial and put it into context with the decision to purchase 26 Rafale-M aircraft under the deal signed with France on 28 April 2025.
Ski Jump Compatible
The Rafale-M was designed for use on the French CATOBAR carrier Charles de Gaulle. India’s INS Vikrant and Vikramaditya utilise a STOBAR system. This means aircraft will accelerate down the deck and utilise a ski jump ramp to provide extra lift.
This was addressed long before the trial in October 2026. In January 2022, Dassault flew the Rafale-M to the Indian Navy’s Shore Based Test Facility at INS Hansa in Goa. Here it performed ski jump takeoffs using a land based replica of the Indian carrier deck. This was part of the trial process as part of the evaluation for the new carrier fighters. Boeing’s F/A-18E/F Super Hornet was also trialled here.
The October 2026 trial demonstrates the aircraft was able to perform an arrested landing on the Vikrant. Showing an important part of the aircraft’s compatibility.
However, comments from Amalantra have raised questions over the takeoff. An image of the first takeoff was analysed and suggested the aircraft tookoff before the ski jump ramp was reached. This suggests the aircraft could not utilise the ski jump, due to it being clean.
This is just an opinion from the image however it draws attention to a valid point. Just because the aircraft can take off from the deck doesn’t mean it can perform a successful launch with a realistic combat loadout.
The key thing will be understanding what fuel, weapon and aircraft weights, along with deck conditions, can be utilised during normal operations.
Aircraft Lift Size Issues
Another consideration is the size of the aircraft. The Rafale-M has a wingspan of around 10.9m and doesn’t have foldable wings. The Vikrant has aircraft lifts of around 10m, whilst Vikramaditya has a central lift of ~9.9m.
This makes transporting the aircraft from the deck to the hangar difficult. The Navy are looking at changes and processes to adapt to the French aircraft. Including removing equipment from the wingtips. [turn450185search4][turn450185search5]
This isn’t just about landing the aircraft. The aircraft needs to be transported, stored, maintained and repaired within the space available. Having an aircraft that can operate from the deck but can’t easily be moved to the hangar will create issues with maintaining the aircraft. Especially in poor weather or when more in depth maintenance is required.
Industrial Benefits for France
The report from ЦАМТО also highlights the industrial benefits. India’s contract includes 22 single seat and 4 double seat Rafale-M aircraft. Along with weapons, simulators, related equipment, training and performance based logistics.
More significantly the deal includes technology transfer to allow for Indian-built weapons to be integrated. A factory will also be set up in India to produce Rafale fuselages. There will also be maintenance, repair and overhaul facilities for engines, sensors and weapons. This was confirmed by the Ministry of Defence when the deal was signed. Dassault Aviation signed production transfer deals with Tata Advanced Systems in June 2025. This will see the Rafale fuselages produced in Hyderabad. Several major sections of the fuselage will be manufactured here. This will mark the first time the Rafale will be produced structurally in India.

evening.title: Windows Server 2028 won't be compatible by default
evening.text:
Microsoft has pushed Windows Server 2028 into public preview, with an eye on beefed-up security, new infrastructure support, and the inevitable nod to AI.

Neil Hinnant, a director on the Windows Server team, talked up the security tweaks. There's a hardened Server Core configuration by default and a new security baseline. "Trusted Launch extends protection to virtual machines," he wrote. "Confidential VM support begins a journey to support integrity-protected runtimes on supported CVM hardware."

Server Core will therefore arrive locked down by default – good news for security, potentially less so for administrators whose existing configurations depend on more permissive settings.

"For years, Windows Server shipped compatible by default," wrote Senior Product Manager Christina Curlette. "Making the server secure was up to you, usually by applying the Security Baseline or your own hardening scripts after setup."

With Windows Server 2028 (and starting from Windows Server Insider Preview build 29706), Server Core will be installed hardened. "Hundreds of security settings are on from first boot," Curlette wrote.

"Because the defaults are now locked down, some things that worked on Windows Server 2025 may not work on Windows Server 2028 without changes. This includes older protocols, legacy authentication, and some management tools and scripts."

For a company obsessed with backward compatibility, this is quite the step. Welcome though the hardening is, administrators will need to test carefully: working on Windows Server 2025 won't guarantee a smooth ride in the brave new world.

AI gets a role on both sides of the security fence: helping uncover vulnerabilities and giving Microsoft another reason to sell servers. Windows Server 2028 is being pitched for running models locally, with support for accelerators such as AMD's Instinct MI350P.

Not every server is destined to babysit a model, however, and the storage changes may be more immediately useful to enterprise administrators. Windows Server 2028 will enable native NVMe storage by default, along with NVMe over TCP and RDMA. Booting from ReFS is also planned, adding another item to the storage upgrade list.

Intune management for Windows Server has also entered preview. Azure Arc, with its cloud-native management workflows, is obviously still around, while Intune brings a more familiar management interface for administrators already using it for endpoints.

Hinnant acknowledged that this was a "major release," and it looks like the security hardening alone will require a good deal of thought from administrators before organizations adopt the eventual production release.

Esben Dochy, Principal Technical Evangelist for SecOps at Lansweeper, told The Register that Microsoft had indicated that the hardened security only applied to new installations. "If that remains in the final release," he said, "in-place upgrades could be easier. The catch is that those servers may also miss out on the new security defaults."

"Hardening is the right direction," he said, "but it will add work for teams moving to Server 2028."

According to Lansweeper’s figures, as of October 2026, Windows Server 2019 ruled the roost with 33 percent. Windows Server 2025 had reached just 7 percent. "From behavior we've seen in the past," said Dochy, "adoption is primarily driven by lifecycle, so until the more used versions start going EOL, I don't expect much adoption, similar to what Server 2025 is experiencing."

Windows Server 2025 remains under extended support until 2034, but Microsoft's direction of travel is clear: beefed-up security by default, a home for AI applications, and Intune management for fleets of servers. ®

evening.text:
This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s

In a New Jersey lab, researchers are trying to sniff every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with chemical analyses to train what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. Its goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.”

Wiltschko claims the model has already achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence” and is helping fragrance brands design new scents. But Osmo has bigger ambitions, from detecting counterfeit goods to diagnosing diseases. Not everyone is convinced its technology can deliver.

How far could an AI-powered sense of smell really take us?

—Amit Katwala

Hydropower hit record lows in the US Southwest this summer

The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration.

Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. But an extreme, prolonged drought has left water levels dangerously low in the region’s two largest reservoirs—and climate change is adding to the pressure.

Find out how climate change is threatening a vital source of renewable power.

—Casey Crownhart

Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of the US grid, helping move power efficiently across long distances. But they’re complicated and in short supply, and their basic design hasn’t changed much in about a century.

As electricity demand rises from EVs, data centers, and more, plans are emerging to modernize these grid staples. Solid-state versions could help ease supply concerns and cut power losses. The technology is still in development, but it could become a crucial part of our future grid.

Police arrest 15 over £1.5M 'we'll recover your losses' scam targeting elderly
evening.text:
Fifteen people have been arrested over an alleged scam that squeezed more money from investment fraud victims by offering to help recover their losses.

City of London Police searched 17 London addresses on November 11 and apprehended 14 men and one woman. All have since been released on bail. Investigators say the suspected fraudsters posed as regulators to persuade previous victims that compensation was available.

Reports submitted through the UK's Report Fraud service helped investigators trace the compensation pitch to around 3,000 recipients since October 2025.

Most victims were elderly, police said. The offers arrived by letter and email, promising redress for earlier investment losses.

City of London Police said the victims were initially targeted by a range of investment scams related to art, carbon credits, land, whisky, wine, and pensions, and that some took place more than a decade prior to their re-victimization.

Targets were directed to a company that demanded a holding fee before supposedly reclaiming their money. Police say those who paid were left further out of pocket.

"Today's action sends a clear message to those who target vulnerable people for financial gain: you will be pursued and will face robust action," said Nik Adams, deputy commissioner at the City of London Police.

"Behind every fraud report is a real person whose trust has been damaged, and in some cases, whose life savings have been stolen. We know the impact of these crimes can be devastating.

"This case highlights the importance of reporting fraud through the Report Fraud service. Information provided by victims helped investigators link reports together, uncover the wider conspiracy, and identify those involved. It is a powerful reminder that every report counts and can play a vital role in bringing offenders to justice."

The investigation also extends beyond London, with police identifying locations linked to the case in Kent and Hertfordshire.

The searches resulted in officers seizing cash, drugs, and other high-value items, including a watch worth around £230,000, with the total haul valued at more than £2 million.

Police put losses identified so far at £1.5 million and expect that figure to rise as the investigation continues.

Knowing the details of an earlier scam doesn't make a caller trustworthy, police warned. That information can be used to sell victims a second fraud.

Report Fraud has also highlighted substantial losses in other scams affecting older people.

Fraudsters exploiting positions of trust stole a reported £93.8 million during 2025/26. People aged 70 and over lost more than £51 million, with relatives, friends, carers, and others entrusted with their finances among the perpetrators. Report Fraud received 3,812 reports in this category.

"The impact of fraud extends far beyond financial loss, especially when it is carried out by those who are trusted by the victim," said Mark Evans, president at the Law Society of England and Wales.

Similarly, at the end of October, Report Fraud said £24.3 million was stolen between January and August 2026 through AI-augmented investment scams, with people aged 60 and over accounting for nearly 80 percent of reports.

However, it's not always the elderly in scammers' crosshairs. Those in the 30-39 age bracket accounted for the most reports in one of the most lucrative frauds affecting Brits in recent times.

evening.text:
In the one light-day that humanity's most distant object has now traveled from Earth, there has been enough time for details about its creation—and what it left behind—to be discovered again.

Voyager 1, which left Earth in 1977 on an initial mission to fly by Jupiter and Saturn (as well as the latter's moon Titan), crossed into interstellar space in 2012. Like its twin (Voyager 2), Voyager 1 carries a "commemorative phonograph record," in part as a nod to the 100th anniversary of the recording medium and as a message from humanity to whoever (or whatever) encounters the spacecraft on its journey through outer space.

About those forgotten bits, ask Glen Swanson. While researching the history of the Golden Record, he uncovered the discs' overlooked second set of operating directions and located the duplicates that were made and distributed almost five decades ago.

evening.title: ULA says Vulcan lacked the oomph to get Amazon satellites to orbit
evening.text:
United Launch Alliance (ULA) says poor booster performance appears to have doomed Sunday's Vulcan mission, which lost an Amazon Leo satellite payload on the rocket's return to flight.

ULA's initial assessment points to trouble almost immediately. "Early indications are that just after liftoff the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance," it said. As a result, stage separation occurred at too low an altitude, and the rocket was not traveling fast enough for the payload to reach orbit.

The second stage appeared to perform well, with its RL10 engines operating as planned, but that wasn't enough to make up for the shortfall, and the mission failed. ULA lost telemetry approximately ten minutes into flight.

An investigation is underway, led by ULA and overseen by the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), which had to activate two Debris Response Areas where debris was falling. The agency directs aircraft to leave these areas, and others are prevented from entering.

Late Wednesday afternoon GMT, ULA posted an update stating that it looks like it might be the fuel supply rather than the BE-4 engines that caused the underperformance of the booster. The company wrote: “Preliminary indications are that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines."

Previous flights had been blighted by problems with the solid rocket boosters, designed to give the rocket a kick at launch. Those issues prompted a stand-down while investigators examined the cause. This time, ULA said: "All indications are that the solid rocket booster performance was nominal, following nozzle improvements implemented for this launch."

Attention therefore turns to Vulcan's liquid-fueled core stage, powered by two Blue Origin BE-4 engines, though that does not establish an engine fault. Fuel delivery or another first-stage system could also be responsible, and the investigation is ongoing.

The BE-4 also powers Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket, which exploded on the launchpad during a ground test in May. In August, Blue Origin boss Dave Limp said that the issue originated at the main oxygen valve on one of the BE-4 engines. Modifications were made to deal with the problem.

The upper stage's apparently normal performance may offer some reassurance to NASA, although the investigation remains at an early stage. The agency dropped the delayed Exploration Upper Stage earlier this year and is pursuing a stretched Centaur V alongside its existing interim cryogenic propulsion stage as options for Artemis IV.

NASA is targeting Artemis IV for early 2028 and Artemis V for later that year.

ULA said: "We truly understand the impact this has on our customers and are committed to returning to flight as safely and quickly as we can."

The failure also dents ULA's otherwise impressive launch record. A predecessor of Vulcan, the Atlas V, has a 100 percent success record for payloads reaching orbit. However, it uses Russian RD-180 engines, a dependency the US wishes to remove. ®
